summary: This standards-track document defines an abstract base YANG data model for network and service topologies and inventories. More specific models for particular technologies are expected to extend it. It gives a common vocabulary for describing nodes, links and how they connect.

eli5.summary: A map shows towns and roads. This is a basic map format for networks that other, more detailed maps can build on.

questions: what is the yang data model for network topologies
how to describe a network topology in yang
how to model network topology in yang
what is a termination point in network topology
subtitle: A generic YANG model that describes networks as layered graphs of nodes, links and termination points.

tldr.problem: Management tools and controllers need one common way to describe network inventories and topologies, including how one network is layered on top of another, without a new model for every technology.
tldr.mechanism: Two YANG modules define a base model: ietf-network holds networks, their supporting (underlay) networks and nodes, and ietf-network-topology adds links and termination points. Technology-specific models extend them by augmentation.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard base model that other topology models build on, such as the Layer 3 model in RFC 8346. Applications can work with any network at a generic level.

today: RFC 8345 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text names RFC 8346 (Layer 3 topologies) as an example of a model that extends it.

sections.title: Why a Base Topology Model
sections.content:
RFC 8345 defines an abstract, or base, YANG data model for network and service topologies and inventories. It is deliberately generic. The details of a particular kind of network are left to other, more specific models that extend this one.

The model has two parts. The first, the ietf-network module, lets you define networks, stack them on top of each other, and keep an inventory of the nodes in each. The second, the ietf-network-topology module, adds links and termination points to describe how those nodes are connected.

The RFC names Layer 2 topologies, Layer 3 topologies (such as unicast IGP, IS-IS and OSPF), traffic engineering data, and transport and service topologies as examples of what extending models can describe. Applications can still operate on the topology of any network at a generic level, and the extended data keeps the same structure.
sections.eli5: Imagine a coloring book with just the outlines: dots for places and lines between them. Anyone can add their own colors and details later, but everybody starts from the same outline.

sections.title: Networks and Nodes
sections.content:
The ietf-network module holds a container with a list of networks. Each network is one list entry, distinguished by a network-id. A network can have one or more types at once (for example L2, L3, OSPF or IS-IS), recorded under a network-types container. In the base model that container is only an augmentation target. Network types SHOULD be presence containers rather than leafs of type empty, so that a hierarchy of subtypes can be shown, such as an OSPF network that is also a Layer 3 unicast IGP network.

A network can list supporting-network entries, which makes it an overlay on top of one or more underlay networks. A network also holds an inventory of node entries, each identified by a node-id inside its network. A node can in turn list supporting-node entries, so a router node might be supported by a route processor node and line card nodes, or a virtual router by a physical device node.

A node does not exist independently of its network. If one device takes part in several networks, it is represented by one node per network. To show that they are the same device, the RFC suggests a "physical" network whose nodes stand for the devices, used as an underlay for the others.
sections.eli5: Think of a school with several maps: one of the classrooms, one of the bus routes. The same teacher appears on both maps as a separate dot, and a master list of real people shows they are the same person.

sections.title: Links and Termination Points
sections.content:
The ietf-network-topology module augments the network model. Each node gets a list of termination points, which anchor links; an example is a physical or logical port or, more generally, an interface. Each network gets a list of links, each identified by a link-id that is unique within the topology.

Links are point-to-point and unidirectional, so each has a source and a destination, and each of those names a node and a termination point on it. Like nodes, links and termination points can map onto underlay counterparts through supporting-link and supporting-termination-point lists.

Bidirectional connections are represented as pairs of unidirectional links, and multipoint networks with pseudonodes, similar to IS-IS. Because a link ends at a single termination point, multihoming and link aggregation are modeled with several point-to-point links and a higher-layer link supported by them.
sections.eli5: Dots are places, and each place has doors. A road always goes from one door to one other door and only one way, so a two-way road is just two one-way roads.

sections.title: Extending the Base Model
sections.content:
To describe a specific kind of network, a new YANG module defines augmentations against both base modules. First it defines a presence container for the new network type and inserts it below network-types. Then it adds node parameters specific to that type, and link and termination point parameters, to the node, link and termination-point lists. These can be made conditional with a when statement on the presence of the network type.

If a network type needs a particular kind of underlay, the module can add constraints on the supporting-network list, but the RFC advises care to avoid excessive constraints. Where network types form a hierarchy, a module for a more specific type augments the module of the more general one.

Mappings stay generic on purpose. The base model does not say whether a termination point is an interface or a node is a device. An augmenting module can add that, for example a leaf of type interface-ref pointing to an interface as defined in RFC 8343.
sections.eli5: It is like a basic Lego plate. Anyone can snap on their own pieces, such as roads or train tracks, without changing the plate itself.

sections.title: Design Decisions
sections.content:
Section 4.4 of the RFC records several choices. The containment structure is kept flat, with lists of nodes, links and termination points not wrapped in separate containers, so that paths stay compact. The model uses YANG groupings so that data can be reused in notifications, at the cost of more complex constraints.

Identifiers for networks, nodes, links and termination points are URIs rather than plain strings. The RFC argues that these objects exist in a larger context, and a URI makes the structure of an identifier explicit and can be fed to a resolver, while strings tend to hide structure that every system must learn separately.

Some mapping data is redundant. If link mappings and each link's termination points are known, the termination point mappings can be derived. The model still lets you configure them explicitly and includes integrity constraints to check consistency.

Network types are modeled as a container of presence containers, not an empty leaf or a leaf-list, so that one network type can refine another like a class hierarchy.
sections.eli5: The authors picked simple rules so the map stays easy to read and easy to grow. Names are like web addresses, so a place can be found even when many maps are combined.

sections.title: Configured and Learned Topologies
sections.content:
Some topology is discovered from the network, while some, such as an overlay, is configured by a client. YANG normally separates configuration data from operational data, but this model puts all data in config true and relies on the datastores of the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342) to tell the cases apart. Discovered data is system controlled and appears in the operational state datastore. Configured data lives in a configuration datastore such as intended, and appears in operational only once it has taken effect. The origin metadata marks discovered data as learned and configured data as intended.

A configured overlay may refer to a supporting node, link or termination point in an underlay. If such a reference dangles, the configured item is removed from the operational state datastore and stays only in the intended one, using the YANG 1.1 require-instance construct. The client application must repair it. A server SHOULD validate supporting references when it receives an overlay configuration, and SHOULD reject requests that refer to objects that do not exist.

The RFC also says the model is meant to work with the ephemeral datastore, and that a network written there MAY refer to a system-controlled one. For networks that do not support NMDA, Appendix B defines two companion modules, ietf-network-state and ietf-network-topology-state, which are read-only mirrors. They SHOULD NOT be supported by implementations that do support NMDA.
sections.eli5: Some parts of the map are drawn by a robot that explores, and some are drawn by you. If you draw a road to a place that is not there, it simply does not show up on the real map until the place appears.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are meant to be accessed with NETCONF or RESTCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH and TLS. The NETCONF access control model (RFC 8341) can limit which users see or change which parts.

The RFC points out two risks. Topology and inventory data reveal the structure of a network, which could help an attacker, and some node identifiers may be tied to devices that belong to specific users. Also, writable data such as client-created overlays can be abused: a malicious client could add or remove networks, nodes, links or termination points, or change supporting references. A configured topology could then be cut or set up inefficiently, which could disrupt services. Learned topologies are protected because the server rejects such attempts, so the RFC says access control must be applied vigorously to prevent misconfiguration by unauthorized clients.
sections.eli5: A map of your town is useful to a burglar, and someone who scribbles on the map can send people the wrong way. So only the right people should be allowed to see it or change it.
